elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Rendered clause inserts "may no more than once per year", which on a literal reading limits inspections per year (potentially calendar year) rather than in any rolling twelve (12) month period; nothing ties the limit to a 12-month look-back.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Retained: "upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice to the Company".
Retained: "during the Company's normal business hours".

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: The inspection right is exercised by "HDI's General Manager", i.e. Vendor personnel; no independent auditor requirement was added.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: No confidentiality obligation on the inspecting person appears in Section 3.4 and none was inserted.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: Clause contemplates inspection of the Company's General Manager's records during the Company's normal business hours, with no off-site-where-possible qualifier added.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: "The fees incurred by HDI in connection with the inspection shall be borne by HDI" — unconditional Vendor cost bearing, more favourable than the 5 percent exception.

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: The right is limited to inspecting "the records of the Company's General Manager reasonably related to the calculation of such payments"; no system-access or remote-access language exists to delete.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: Inserted operative words: "may no more than once per year, upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice" — a frequency cap of one inspection per year now binds HDI.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Existing "no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice to the Company" exceeds the 15-day floor.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: "The fees incurred by HDI in connection with the inspection shall be borne by HDI" — Vendor bears cost unconditionally, with no underpayment shift-back, which satisfies and exceeds the element.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete on the rendered language: the inserted once-per-year cap supplies the only missing element, and the retained 30-day notice and unconditional HDI-borne cost already met the notice and cost elements.

Preferred level is not reached: the inspection is still performed by HDI's own General Manager (no independent, confidentiality-bound auditor) and there is no off-site-where-possible qualifier. To reach preferred the drafter would need to require an independent auditor bound by written confidentiality obligations and off-site inspection where possible.

Drafting nit (rationale-level, not a fallback failure): "once per year" could be read as a calendar-year rather than rolling limit; "no more than once in any twelve (12) month period" would close that gap and simultaneously satisfy the preferred frequency element. The inserted phrase also reads awkwardly before "have the right to inspect"; consider "may, no more than once in any twelve (12) month period and upon no less than thirty (30) days prior written notice to the Company, inspect...".

Minimality is satisfied: a single frequency phrase was inserted; the favourable business-hours limit, 30-day notice, narrow records scope and HDI-borne cost were all retained unchanged, and no extras (procedures, expense allocation, survival) were added.

Intent is preserved: the clause remains HDI's records-verification right tied to calculation of the payments, with no undefined terms, dangling cross-references or contradictory retained sentence introduced.

The "deviation" characterisation is sound: before the edit the inspection right had no frequency limit, which is walk-away territory (unlimited audits) and fails the fallback, so a redline was warranted rather than a rationale-only note.
